backups.name: West Ridge
gear: Ice axe & crampons (snow and small glacier slopes from Crescent Creek Basin to the col)
Glacier travel rope + crevasse-rescue kit (2-3 person rope team)
Light alpine rock rack for the ridge climbing
Helmet (loose rock typical of unrepeated Southern Pickets lines)
hazards: Loose rock, typical of unrepeated Picket Range lines.
Documented by a single 2017 first-ascent trip report — no grade, pitch count, or length is recorded, so treat all difficulty and gear information as unknown.
Deep in the Southern Pickets: a long, committing wilderness approach with route-finding throughout and no realistic prospect of quick outside help.
Afternoon weather deterioration is a recurring hazard on this peak.
backups.overview: A 2017 first-ascent line up Ottohorn's west ridge, climbed during the same outing that established two nearby new routes ('Beep' and 'Honk') in the Southern Pickets. Its grade, pitch count and length are not recorded.
backups.beta: Established alongside two other new Southern Pickets routes in July 2017; beyond the trip-report title and date, no further route beta (grade, protection, or descent) is publicly available.
backups.turnaround: Set a hard turnaround before you leave camp and honour it. Two conditions should stop you regardless of the clock: fresh rockfall debris or visibly unstable blocks on the last 30 ft of the summit ridge (back off and take the north-side variation or go home — one party found exactly this and made the right call), and a moat or bergschrund below the col that has opened enough that you are not confident of recrossing it in the afternoon when it is softer. Weather turnaround: if cloud is filling Crescent Creek Basin, go down while you can still see the Barrier — routefinding across it in a whiteout on loose grassy ledges is how people get hurt here. Because the col is only about an hour from camp, there is almost never a good reason to push a marginal call on this peak.
backups.rock_grade: Class 3-4 (a 5.7 variation exists on the north side of the summit blocks)
backups.rappels: None on the east ridge, which is normally downclimbed to the col. The south-side gully below the col needs none in early season while snow fills it; later in the summer, as the snow melts back, parties rappel the chockstone and moats at its top from fixed anchors before kicking down the remaining snow. Parties who take the 5.7 variation on the north side of the summit blocks generally make one or two single-rope rappels off slung blocks to regain the ridge. If you continue north out of the col instead of returning to Crescent Creek Basin (i.e. toward the Mustard Glacier and Picket Pass), budget three or more rappels off improvised anchors — a 2011 party built theirs from a driven piton, a slung block and a nut in a constriction, then rappelled the broken couloir and glacier spilling off the north side.
backups.face: Crescent Creek Spires — south side, from Crescent Creek Basin via the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn (Otto-Himmel) col
backups.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek cross-country zones are walk-up only, issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
backups.comms: Assume no cell coverage. The Goodell Creek trailhead sits in a deep valley beside SR 20 near Newhalem with marginal service at best, and there is none on the climbers' path, in Terror Basin or in Crescent Creek Basin. Line-of-sight from high points on the crest occasionally produces a bar or two toward the Skagit valley, but it is not something to plan around. Carry a satellite messenger or PLB — NPS climbing guidance for North Cascades is explicit that parties here must be self-reliant, and a rescue in the Southern Pickets is a multi-day helicopter operation dependent on weather windows. Leave a detailed itinerary with someone at home and file your route with the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount when you pick up the permit.
backups.descent: Downclimb the east ridge back to the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col, then descend the snow south into Crescent Creek Basin and reverse the approach over the Barrier.

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek / Upper Goodell Group Camp trailhead (SR-20, Newhalem)

timing.recommendedStart: From a Crescent Creek Basin camp, leave at first light (roughly 05:00-06:00) so the snow up to the Otto-Himmel col is still firm and the moat crossing is at its most solid, and so you are back at camp with the whole afternoon in hand. A pre-dawn alpine start is not necessary for the climb itself — the col is only about an hour above camp — but it matters if you intend to link Himmelhorn or Mount Terror the same day, or to recross the Barrier and keep descending.

backups.detailed_rack: Glacier travel gear for the snow and small glacier slopes from Crescent Creek Basin to the col, plus a light alpine rock rack (assorted nuts + small-to-mid cams ~0.3-2in) and slings for rock steps on the ridge; a 60m rope covers rappelling loose terrain near the Otto-Himmel col.
what_to_bring: North Cascades backcountry permit, picked up in person at Marblemount, since the zones here are walk-up only
Satellite messenger or PLB — there is no cell coverage on any part of this route
Bear canister or a proper hang bag (NPS food-storage rules apply)
Blue bags for human waste on snow and bare rock — never bury it in snow
3-4 L water capacity; the climbers' path has essentially no water for 5,000 ft
GPX or waypoint for the stone arrow at ~1,700 ft where the Terror Creek path leaves the roadbed
Approach shoes for the roadbed plus boots that take crampons
Full storm shell and insulation — maritime squalls hit the Pickets even in August
Sun protection and glacier glasses for the snow basins
Trekking poles for the 5,000 ft climbers' path and the brutal descent of it
Map of the Barrier crossing; it is the single easiest place on the trip to get cliffed out
pro_tips: Camp in Crescent Creek Basin, not Terror Basin. One party reached the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col in about an hour from a Crescent Creek Basin camp — that turns Ottohorn into a short morning instead of a full day with a Barrier crossing at each end.

The turnoff from the Goodell Creek roadbed to the Terror Creek climbers' path is marked only by a stone arrow on the ground at about 1,700 ft, roughly 3.5-4 miles in. Waypoint it before you leave home; people walk past it every season.
Go while there is still snow in the basins. The Otto-Himmel col is straightforward when snow-filled and turns into loose, tricky low-fifth-class rock once it melts out.

Nobody comes all this way for Ottohorn alone. Plan it as one of several summits from a single Crescent Creek Basin camp — Himmelhorn's Wild Hair Crack, Mount Terror and Twin Needles all share the same base.

Treat the last 30 ft as a rockfall zone rather than a scramble. A 2011 party found the standard finish had collapsed into fresh unstable blocks and went around the corner onto two juggy 5.7 pitches instead — the harder line was the safer one that day.
Carry a couple of pitons and be prepared to leave gear. Anchors in this cirque are slung blocks, nuts and driven pins, not fixed stations.
Scout the moat below the col on the way up and remember exactly where you crossed it; it will be softer and wider on the way down.

Pick up the permit and current conditions in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center (360-854-7200) — the rangers there track snow levels on the Terror Creek path and the state of the Barrier.
Build a spare day into the trip. Parties on the Southern Picket traverse routinely burn one to squalls, and both the Barrier and the climbers' path are markedly more dangerous wet.
watch_out: The final ~30 ft to the summit ridge has produced active rockfall; blocks that look welded in place are not.
The south side of the Otto-Himmel col is the friendly side. The north side can demand loose 5th class or rappels once the snow goes, and it commits you to the Mustard Glacier.
Moats and bergschrunds where the snow meets rock below the col open into overhanging pits by late season — one party had to jump one and axe their way out the far side.
The Barrier crossing at about 6,100 ft is 'serious Class 3' on steep, loose, grassy ledges. It is the real crux of the trip and it is not a place to slip.
This is arguably the most isolated terrain in the contiguous United States. A broken ankle in Crescent Creek Basin is a multi-day, weather-dependent helicopter problem.
The Terror Creek climbers' path gains roughly 5,000 ft with almost no water between the creek and treeline — carry it.
Skagit Gneiss in the Pickets swings between excellent and appalling within a single pitch; test everything, and keep the party out of each other's fall line.
backups.pro_needs: Protection needs are minimal but the rock quality is the variable. On the standard Class 3-4 east ridge most parties place nothing at all, or slings over blocks and horns for a moving belay through the final step. If the direct summit finish looks loose, the north-side 5.7 variation takes conventional small-to-medium gear in solid, juggy rock and is the safer choice despite the higher grade. The larger protection problem is the snow below the col — a bergschrund and moat that grows through the season — so bring the glacier kit even though the rock rack is trivial.
backups.best_season: Mid-July through mid-September is the working window, and earlier in it is generally better. The whole trip is easier with snow: the traverse of Terror Basin, the Barrier crossing and the slopes up to the Otto-Himmel col are all straightforward when snow-filled, and the col specifically is described as easy when snowy and as loose, tricky low-fifth-class rock once melted out. Against that, a big snow year can leave the Terror Basin approach and the climbers' path buried and the basins short of running water in early July. Late July and August are the usual compromise — settled maritime high pressure, the climbers' path melted out, and enough snow left in the basins for travel. By September the col and the moats below it are at their worst, though the summit ridge is at its driest. Outside that window this is a full winter expedition into the most isolated terrain in the lower 48, with an avalanche-prone maritime snowpack.
backups.approach: There is no trail to this peak; the approach is the trip. From SR 20 just west of Newhalem, turn north opposite the North Cascades Visitor Center entrance road, go left at the immediate T-junction, past a gravel quarry, then right and uphill on a narrow but well-graded gravel road to the signed Goodell Creek climbers' trailhead (48.6866, -121.2712, about 600 ft). Follow the old roadbed up Goodell Creek for roughly 3.5-4 miles. At about 1,700 ft a stone arrow on the ground marks the unsigned turnoff for the Terror Creek climbers' path — it is easy to walk straight past it, so waypoint it in advance. From the arrow the boot-beaten path climbs relentlessly and steeply up the hillside, gaining about 5,000 ft with essentially no reliable water, to timberline at 5,000-5,200 ft. Above treeline make a rising traverse over meadows, slabs and snowfields toward a 6,200 ft saddle; the standard Terror Basin camp sits about 400 ft below the saddle at roughly 5,800 ft. One party took about 6.5 hours from the trailhead to Terror Basin. For Ottohorn you must keep going west: traverse Terror Basin holding roughly the 6,000 ft contour, then cross the Barrier — the ridge dividing Terror Basin from Crescent Creek Basin — at about 6,100 ft. The Barrier crossing is the non-technical crux of the whole trip: steep, loose, grassy 'serious Class 3' ledges where a slip is not survivable. Drop into Crescent Creek Basin and camp at about 6,200 ft (a good alternative camp sits at 6,400 ft on the Chopping Block ridge overlooking the basin). From that camp, snow and small glacier slopes lead northwest in about an hour to the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col at roughly 7,400 ft, where the route proper begins. Note on the numbers: the listed 7,240 ft is the net trailhead-to-summit gain from recorded elevations; the Barrier crossing and the Terror Basin traverse add several hundred feet of extra up-and-down each way, and the near-identical Goodell Creek / Terror Basin / Barrier approach to Mount Terror is recorded at 20 miles and 10,000 ft round trip.
backups.descent_text: Reverse the east ridge — 200-250 ft of blocky Class 3 with a short Class 4 step, downclimbed by most parties. If you climbed the 5.7 variation on the north side of the summit blocks, one or two single-rope rappels off slung blocks put you back on the ridge crest; back the anchor up, because the rock here has proven itself capable of moving. From the Otto-Himmel col descend the snow and glacier slopes south back into Crescent Creek Basin. The critical detail here is the moat and bergschrund where the snow meets the rock: it is a non-event when snow-filled in early season and can become an overhanging pit by August. One party descending the equivalent feature on the north side had to jump a large overhanging moat and then climb out the far side with an ice axe. Scout the crossing on the way up and remember where it was; late in the season parties rappel this upper section from fixed anchors. Do NOT descend north out of the col unless you are deliberately continuing toward the Mustard Glacier and Picket Pass — that side takes multiple rappels off improvised anchors down a broken couloir and glacier. From Crescent Creek Basin, recross the Barrier at about 6,100 ft (the steep grassy ledges are considerably worse downhill-facing and tired), traverse Terror Basin at roughly the 6,000 ft contour, then drop the 5,000 ft climbers' path to the stone arrow at 1,700 ft and follow the old roadbed out to Goodell Creek. Give the descent of the climbers' path real respect — it is steep, loose, brushy and hard on knees, and the exit is where most parties are moving slowest.
backups.bail: There is no quick exit from Crescent Creek Basin — every retreat goes back over the Barrier into Terror Basin and down the Goodell Creek climbers' path, so plan on a full day out from high camp regardless of what has gone wrong. On the route itself, bailing is easy and cheap: the east ridge can be downclimbed anywhere back to the Otto-Himmel col, and the col is only about an hour of snow above camp. If the summit blocks look freshly loose, retreating from the col and going to Himmelhorn or Terror instead costs nothing. Do not use the north side of the col as an escape — it drops onto the Mustard Glacier and commits you to multiple rappels off improvised gear and, ultimately, to an exit via Picket Pass and the Big Beaver or Access Creek valleys, which is a far bigger undertaking than walking back over the Barrier.

pitch_detail.notes: From camp at roughly 6,200 ft, climb snow and small glacier slopes northwest toward the notch between Ottohorn and Himmelhorn. About an hour from a Crescent Creek Basin camp. Rope up for glacier travel; crampons and axe. Early season this is a straightforward snow plod, late season it becomes bare ice and rubble.
pitch_detail.pitch: Section 1 — Crescent Creek Basin to below the col

pitch_detail.grade: Steep snow, or loose low 5th class late season
pitch_detail.notes: The transition from snow to rock at roughly 7,400 ft. Trivial when snow-filled; by August the moat can be overhanging and the exit onto the col can require loose fifth-class moves. The south (Crescent Creek) side is markedly friendlier than the north. Scout the crossing here for the descent.
pitch_detail.pitch: Section 2 — bergschrund / moat and exit onto the Otto-Himmel col

pitch_detail.notes: From the col, blocky scrambling west up the ridge crest on Skagit Gneiss. Most parties move unroped. Good holds interspersed with detached blocks — keep the party out of each other's fall line.

pitch_detail.grade: Class 3-4 (or 5.7 variation on the north side)
pitch_detail.notes: The final step to the summit at 7,840 ft. Graded Class III by the 1961 first-ascent party and Class 4 by the 2003 enchainment party. In 2011 the direct finish was found to be an active fresh-rockfall zone about 30 ft below the ridge; that party avoided it by moving around the corner onto two juggy 5.7 pitches. Judge it on the day and rope up if there is any doubt.

backups.itinerary: Day 1 — Goodell Creek trailhead (600 ft) to Terror Basin camp (5,800 ft), about 6.5 hours; 3.5-4 miles of old roadbed then 5,000 ft of climbers' path. Day 2 — traverse Terror Basin at the 6,000 ft contour, cross the Barrier at about 6,100 ft, and camp in Crescent Creek Basin (6,200 ft) or on the Chopping Block ridge at 6,400 ft; a short day that leaves the afternoon for scouting the line to the col. Day 3 — summit day: about an hour of snow and glacier from camp to the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col (7,400 ft), then the east ridge to the summit (7,840 ft) and back to camp; almost everyone links a second objective from the same camp (Himmelhorn's Wild Hair Crack, Mount Terror, or Twin Needles) rather than making a dedicated trip for Ottohorn. Day 4 — recross the Barrier and descend to the trailhead. Build a weather day into the plan: parties on the full traverse routinely lose a day to squalls, and the Barrier and the climbers' path are both much worse wet.

access.fees: Summer backcountry permits cost $10 per person plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee; youth 15 and under are free. Fees apply mid-May through early October; permits are free from early October to mid-May. There is no park entrance fee and no parking fee on North Cascades National Park land.
access.permit: A backcountry/wilderness permit is required for every overnight stay, including bivouacs — which means every realistic ascent of this peak. The Terror Basin and Crescent Creek cross-country zones cannot be booked ahead: their permits are walk-up only, issued in person the day of or the day before your trip. The Wilderness Information Center at 7280 Ranger Station Road, Marblemount WA 98267 (360-854-7200) issues permits, lends bear canisters and gives current conditions.
access.closures: No standing closure on this approach. Practical constraints instead: no campfires anywhere in the backcountry zones (stoves only), food must be stored in a bear canister or hung, human waste must be packed out in blue bags on snow and bare rock and never buried in snow or crevasses, and all flagging and webbing left behind counts as trash. Cutting vegetation is illegal and citable. Check with the Wilderness Information Center for temporary closures before each trip.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park (National Park Service) — the Southern Picket Range cross-country zone. Trailhead and approach are within the North Cascades National Park Complex.
access.passRequired: No Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass is needed to park at the Goodell Creek climbers' trailhead — it is on park land, where NPS charges no entry or parking fee. (Note that many other North Cascades-area trailheads on adjacent Forest Service land do require a Northwest Forest Pass.)

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades NP backcountry permit for the cross-country zone, with a fee
overnight_permit.where: This zone is walk-up only: get the permit in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, the day of or the day before your trip.

road.name: Goodell Creek Campground access road off SR 20 (North Cascades Highway) at Newhalem
road.status: Open — paved SR 20 to Newhalem, then a short gravel spur past a gravel quarry to a developed climbers' trailhead with parking and a sign noting this is a climbers' trail, not a hikers' trail. Passable to any passenger car.
road.driveNote: From Marblemount follow SR 20 east about 14 miles to Newhalem. Turn north opposite the North Cascades Visitor Center entrance road, go left at the immediate T-junction, continue past a gravel quarry where the pavement ends, then take the right fork uphill on a narrow but well-graded gravel road; the trailhead is on the right within about a mile. Trailhead at 48.6866, -121.2712, roughly 600 ft.
road.seasonalGate: None affecting this approach. SR 20's winter closure gates sit east of Newhalem — the initial closure is between the Ross Dam trailhead (MP 134) and the Silver Star gate (MP 171), moving down to the Newhalem gate (MP 120) and Early Winters (MP 178) in deep winter. Access to Goodell Creek from Marblemount and the west is open year-round.

climate.fall: Early September can be superb: dry rock on the summit ridge, stable air, fewer bugs. The trade-off is that the Otto-Himmel col and the moats below it are at their most melted-out and awkward, and the first Pacific fronts of the autumn arrive without much warning. After late September, storms and short days make the approach and the Barrier crossing dangerous.
climate.spring: Deep, consolidating maritime snowpack. Wet, heavy snow and high avalanche danger on the basins and the couloirs off the crest; cornices along the Southern Picket ridgeline. The Terror Creek climbers' path is usually snow-covered and the approach becomes a serious snow-travel undertaking rather than a hike.
climate.summer: The season. Late July through August brings the most settled high pressure, the climbers' path melts out, and the basins still hold enough snow to make the Terror Basin traverse, the Barrier and the slopes to the col straightforward. Squalls still come through — parties on multi-day traverses routinely lose a day to rain and wind even in August.
climate.winter: Full expedition conditions. Heavy maritime snowfall, high and persistent avalanche danger, and a 5,000 ft approach path buried under snow with no reliable route through the Barrier. Essentially unvisited in winter.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate. Most weather originates over the Pacific and is driven northeast into the Cascades, where orographic lift wrings out heavy precipitation on the western slopes — the Pickets sit right in the firing line. Temperatures are moderated by the maritime influence and rarely drop below 0F or exceed 80F. Expect the range to make its own weather: clear valleys below and cloud sitting on the crest is a normal Picket day.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC 'West Slopes North' avalanche forecast zone.

emergency.notes: Plan as if no outside help is coming quickly. The Picket Range is among the most isolated terrain in the contiguous United States, there is no cell coverage anywhere on the route, and a rescue from Crescent Creek Basin depends on a helicopter and a weather window — realistically a multi-day proposition. Carry a satellite messenger or PLB, leave a detailed itinerary with a contact at home, and register your route with the Wilderness Information Center when collecting the permit. Self-rescue capability (crevasse and moat extraction, improvised rappel anchors, the ability to get an injured partner back over the Barrier) is the practical minimum standard for this trip.
emergency.county: Whatcom County, Washington (the Goodell Creek trailhead and the SR 20 drive are in Whatcom County; the nearest hospital is over the line in Skagit County)
emergency.rangerStation: North Cascades National Park Wilderness Information Center, 7280 Ranger Station Road, Marblemount WA 98267 — 360-854-7200. Permits, current conditions, bear canister loans and trip-planning advice.
emergency.nearestHospital: PeaceHealth United General Medical Center, 2000 Hospital Drive, Sedro-Woolley WA 98284 — 24/7 Level IV emergency department, ED phone 360-856-6021. It is the critical-access hospital serving Marblemount and the upper Skagit; anything major will be transferred onward.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: 911 for emergencies. Whatcom County Sheriff's Office non-emergency dispatch: 360-676-6911. The WCSO runs search and rescue for the Southern Pickets.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through August, with the Terror Basin path melted out but enough basin snow left to ease the col

July.reason: Early July can still bury the approach, but by late month the path is clear and snow still fills the Otto-Himmel col.

June.reason: The Terror Creek path and basins are buried, avalanche slopes loom over the Barrier traverse, and meltwater is scarce.

August.reason: Settled high pressure, a melted-out climbers' path and enough snow in the basins for fast travel to the col.

October.reason: Early storms and short days on a committing route in the most remote part of the Pickets; walk-up permits end with the season.

September.reason: The summit ridge is driest, but the col melts to loose low-fifth-class rock and the moats below it are at their worst.

approach_logistics.trailhead: Goodell Creek / Upper Goodell Group Camp trailhead (SR-20, Newhalem)

climbing_route.label: Scramble from the Himmelhorn-Ottohorn col
climbing_route.notes: From the col the summit is reported as easy scrambling — most accounts call the peak class 3, with a short class 4 step, and describe it as one of the few Southern Picket summits that is not fifth class. Parties have climbed it from the col in roughly an hour round trip, some without taking rope or rack out of camp. Picket rock is broken and the col itself is loose, so helmets and careful block-testing matter more than the grade suggests; the col is also the retreat point, and getting back down into Crescent Creek Basin late in the season can be harder than the scramble above.

climbing_route.label: Rockfall scar below the summit ridge
climbing_route.notes: At least one party found the easy line broke into a fresh rockfall zone about 30 ft below the summit ridge and backed off rather than cross it, returning with a rope and climbing a roped alternative of about two pitches of juggy 5.7 to the top. Treat this as conditions-dependent rather than fixed: the scar is recent enough that the terrain here may have changed again, and a scramble party arriving without gear may find no acceptable line through the unstable blocks. Carry enough to retreat or to protect a short 5th-class variation, and do not commit to the last 100 ft until you can see it.

bivy.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
bivy.permit: This is the separate Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
bivy.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is legally awkward: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is not on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is walk-up only — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Stump Hollow bench
bivy.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
bivy.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

bivy.name: High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
bivy.notes: The western summits — the Twin Needles, Ottohorn, Himmelhorn and Frenzel Spitz — are far enough along the crest that a party working from a basin camp faces a very long day, so some take a bivouac high on the traverse instead. These are improvised spots rather than established sites, and quality varies from a decent gravel bench to a night sitting on a ledge. There is no shelter and no water, so this only makes sense with a settled forecast and a party willing to move fast the next morning.
bivy.water: No dependable source. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs: carry water up or melt snow, and expect nothing at all once the summer snow has gone.
bivy.permit: Still inside a cross-country zone and still requires a wilderness permit with the night assigned to the correct zone. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, keep 100 ft from water, no fires, and carry waste out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: One party, and often only a ledge or a gravel patch for two people

backups.name: Southeast Route

backups.overview: The Ottohorn is a slender granite spire in the Southern Pickets, rising directly across the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col from its larger neighbor Himmelgeisterhorn, deep in North Cascades National Park's Crescent Creek Basin. It was first climbed on September 10, 1961 by Ed Cooper, Glen Denny, Joan Firey, Joe Firey, and George Whitmore via the east ridge from the col (Class III) — the same trip that put up Himmelgeisterhorn and Frenzel Spitz, all three reportedly named after labels the Fireys peeled off a mustard bottle carried on the approach. One of the range's more obscure summits, Ottohorn is rarely climbed alone; most parties tag it as part of a Crescent Creek Basin enchainment with Himmelgeisterhorn and/or Frenzel Spitz.
backups.beta: From the Otto-Himmel Col (reached via Stump Hollow trail from Goodell Creek trailhead), ascend the east ridge directly to the summit. Early season (June–July): route is primarily snow with Class II-III scrambling near summit; descent is straightforward on consolidated snow. Mid-season (July–August): snow transitions to exposed rock; negotiable as Class III with careful foot placement. Late season (August–September): loose, tricky 5th class scrambling through chossy rock and talus fields. Final approach to summit features a fresh rockfall zone approximately 30 feet below summit ridge; experienced alpinists rope-protect the 5.7 pitches or navigate unstable terrain carefully. Route is approximately 500–700 vertical feet from col to summit.
backups.turnaround: Because the col crossing and east ridge get looser as the day warms, and because the Barrier/Terror Creek exit is easy to lose in poor visibility, most parties set a firm early-afternoon turnaround from Crescent Creek Basin camp to guarantee daylight for the return to camp.
backups.face: Southeast side, reached from the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col
backups.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek cross-country zones are walk-up only, issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
backups.comms: No reliable cell service in the Southern Pickets backcountry; parties should carry a satellite messenger/communicator for emergencies.
backups.descent: Reverse the route: downclimb/scramble back to the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col and descend its south side into Crescent Creek Basin.
obj_haz: loose rock at and above the col
bergschrund/moat at the col late season

backups.detailed_rack: Bring a light rack of passive protection (nuts, hexes) and a few cams (size 00–2) for securing belays or protecting the 5.7 pitches used to bypass rockfall zones. Slings and cordage for creating anchors in scree and rock. Screwgate carabiners for safety. Most of the route is Class III solo scramble; the 5.7 option is backup for significant weather delays or if rockfall zone is extremely active.
what_to_bring: Helmet — loose rock is the norm throughout the Southern Pickets
Light alpine rock rack for low-5th-class to 5.7 terrain
Sturdy approach footwear for brush, slide alder, and talus on the Barrier
Ice axe (and possibly light traction) for lingering snow on the Barrier and Otto-Himmel col into July
pro_tips: Most parties climb Ottohorn as part of a one-day enchainment with Himmelgeisterhorn and/or Frenzel Spitz from a Crescent Creek Basin camp — plan for a full day out.
At the stone cairn on the Goodell Creek approach, staying straight (not turning onto the more obvious trail) keeps you headed for Crescent Creek Basin instead of Terror Basin.
Carry a satellite communicator — there is no cell coverage in Crescent Creek Basin or on the approach.
A steeper 2-pitch 5.7 variation on the southeast side has also been reported (Hilden-Holsten-Wertkin party) for parties wanting more sustained climbing.
watch_out: The north side of the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col turns loose, exposed low-5th-class scrambling by late season as snow melts out — the south side is the friendlier crossing.
The Barrier crossing between Terror and Crescent Creek basins has turned back parties in poor visibility; don't underestimate route-finding on the brushy ridge crest.
Rock quality on Southern Pickets summits is notoriously loose — test holds and manage rockfall exposure for partners below.
backups.pro_needs: A light alpine rock rack is sufficient for the scattered low-5th-class to 5.7 moves; belays are typically natural gear anchors rather than fixed stations.
backups.best_season: Mid-July through early September is the reliable window. Snow often lingers on the Barrier crossing and in the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col into July, and by early September shortening days and unsettled weather make this remote objective riskier — most parties target a tight late-July-to-August window.
backups.approach: From the Goodell Creek trailhead (~600 ft, reached via the gravel road that forks off Hwy 20 across from Newhalem and dead-ends at a gravel pit — there's parking but no trailhead sign), follow the old abandoned logging roadbed paralleling the true-left/east bank of Goodell Creek. The first ~1.5 miles thread through dozens of downed trees and washouts on the roadbed before a real, if faint, trail emerges in the timber above; tread then levels out around 1,100 ft for roughly a mile. Around mile 3.5 (~1,700 ft) the trail crosses a stream — the last easy, reliable water for a long stretch — near a small campsite and a cairn marking the unsigned climbers' path up 'The Barrier,' the forested spur ridge that separates the Goodell/Terror Creek drainage from Crescent Creek Basin; fill bottles here. From the cairn the path steepens hard: a traverse around 3,200 ft, a talus field near 4,000 ft, a rock band around 4,800 ft, then a steep, brush-choked gully (early-season snow/ice up to ~35°) to a rocky streambed near 5,200 ft. Above that, heather benches and slabs lead to the crest of The Barrier, a ~6,200 ft notch that is the high point of the approach and the site of a common bivy. From the notch, descend ~250 ft into 'Stump Hollow,' the gentle basin between The Barrier and the Chopping Block, then contour on a long, rising traverse across the snow, slabs, and talus of Crescent Creek Basin — holding roughly the 5,800 ft level — to a camp near Mount Terror/Himmelhorn (around 7-9 miles and 6,000-6,500 ft of gain from the trailhead, consistent with this route's ~28 km round-trip distance). From camp, continue the rising traverse of Crescent Creek Basin toward the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col; crampon up the final snow/scree pitch to the col itself, which turns to loose, chossy class 3-4 scrambling once melted out late-season, with an overhanging boulder near the top sometimes forcing a chossy class 3/4 bypass on the left. A North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for the Crescent Creek Basin zone is required. Both The Barrier crossing and the basin traverse involve real route-finding on an unsigned, easily-lost climbers' path through heather and talus, and creek crossings near the trailhead can run high and fast on hot, high-snowmelt afternoons.
backups.descent_text: Descend the Southeast Route by reversing the east ridge back down to the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col — a few pitches of low-5th-class downclimbing/scrambling to the notch. From the col, the standard return for this route is down the south side, back into Crescent Creek Basin: this is the easier, non-technical line (snow early season, loose class 3-4 talus/scree scrambling once late-season melt strips the snow) and does not require rappelling under normal conditions. If coverage is thin and a section of the loose downclimb feels too exposed, some parties back it off with a single short rappel off a sling on a natural anchor (block/horn) rather than downclimb it, but this is not the norm. Note that the north side of the col is a different, and harder, proposition and is not part of this route's own descent — parties continuing a traverse toward Himmelhorn/Mustard Glacier descend that side via one single-rope rappel from an established rap station about 150 ft below the col onto the Mustard Glacier (or, when well filled-in, a steep snow couloir); don't confuse that crossing with the Southeast Route's own walk-off. From Crescent Creek Basin, reverse the approach: traverse back to the base of The Barrier, regain the ~250 ft to the 6,200 ft notch, then descend the steep gully/talus/heather line back down to the Goodell Creek trail and out to the trailhead. Watch for loose rock in the gully below the Barrier notch and for creek crossings running high on hot afternoons. To continue on to Frenzel Spitz, descend roughly 500 ft from Ottohorn's north side, per the original 1961 first-ascent account.
backups.bail: Retreat is a straightforward reversal down the east ridge/southeast line back to the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col; most parties can downclimb rather than needing to abandon gear, though the col's north-side descent gets loose and rotten by late summer.

climate.fall: Shortening weather windows; early snow can return to the col and upper ridge by late September.
climate.spring: Heavy snowpack, high avalanche hazard, approach largely impassable for the standard climbers' route.
climate.summer: Primary climbing window (Jul–Sep); still subject to afternoon thunderstorms and periods of persistent low cloud/rain typical of the North Cascades.
climate.winter: Not a viable climbing season; heavy snow and avalanche terrain throughout the approach and route.
climate.typical: Maritime-influenced alpine climate — the Southern Pickets sit close enough to Puget Sound moisture that even summer weather windows can turn quickly. This zone is not covered by NWAC's avalanche forecast; check NWS Bellingham point forecasts and mountain-specific forecasts before committing.

bySeason.fall: Short weather windows after early September; days shorten fast and the brushy approach turns miserable in rain.
bySeason.spring: Approach is still heavily snow-covered; not a realistic season for this route.
bySeason.summer: Best/driest window, but snow often lingers on the Barrier crossing and in the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col into July; afternoon thunderstorms are a real hazard on exposed ridgelines.
bySeason.winter: Effectively inaccessible for climbing — deep snow and avalanche terrain on the approach, though Goodell Creek Road stays reachable off WA-20.

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek, the Barrier notch and Stump Hollow, then the Crescent Creek Basin traverse to the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col
approach_variants.notes:
From the Goodell Creek trailhead at about 600 ft, reached via the gravel road that forks off Hwy 20 across from Newhalem and dead-ends at a gravel pit with parking but no trailhead sign, follow the old logging roadbed along the east bank of Goodell Creek. The first 1.5 miles thread through dozens of downed trees and washouts before a faint trail emerges in the timber; the tread then levels around 1,100 ft for roughly a mile.

Around mile 3.5, at about 1,700 ft, the trail crosses a stream, the last easy reliable water for a long stretch, near a small campsite and a cairn marking the unsigned climbers' path up the Barrier. Fill bottles there.

From the cairn the path steepens hard: a traverse around 3,200 ft, a talus field near 4,000 ft, a rock band around 4,800 ft, then a steep brush-choked gully with early-season snow or ice to about 35 degrees, to a rocky streambed near 5,200 ft. Heather benches and slabs then lead to the crest of the Barrier, a roughly 6,200 ft notch that is the high point of the approach and a common bivy. From the notch, descend about 250 ft into Stump Hollow, then contour on a long rising traverse across Crescent Creek Basin holding roughly the 5,800 ft level to a camp near Mount Terror and Himmelhorn.

A North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for the Crescent Creek Basin zone is required.
hazards: A steep brush-choked gully with early-season snow or ice to about 35 degrees on the Barrier climb
An overhanging boulder near the col forcing a loose exposed bypass
A moat at the col that can become an overhanging pit by August
A fresh rockfall scar reported about 30 ft below the summit ridge
The north side of the col takes multiple rappels off improvised anchors; do not descend it by mistake
Steep grassy ledges on the Barrier that are considerably worse downhill-facing and tired
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The route begins at the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col and you crampon the last of the way there. From camp, continue the rising traverse across Crescent Creek Basin toward the col, and crampon up the final snow and scree pitch to the col itself. Once melted out late season that last pitch turns to loose, chossy class 3-4 scrambling, with an overhanging boulder near the top sometimes forcing a chossy class 3 or 4 bypass on the left.

So the overhanging boulder is the arrival marker: one block near the top of the gully, passed on its left, and then the col. The route text stops at the col because the col is the start.

The negative test, and it is the most important line here: from the col, this route goes up the east ridge and its walk-off returns down the south side, back into Crescent Creek Basin. The north side of the col is a different and harder proposition. Parties continuing a traverse toward Himmelhorn and the Mustard Glacier descend that side by a single-rope rappel from an established station about 150 ft below the col, or a steep snow couloir when well filled in. If you are looking down at a glacier and rigging a rappel, you are on the wrong side of the col for this route.

Confirm on the climb, and the measurements are small: from the col the summit is reported as easy scrambling, class 3, and parties have done it from the col in roughly an hour round trip, some without taking rope or rack out of camp. It is one of the few Southern Picket summits that is not fifth class. If you are on sustained fifth class you are not on the standard line.

One conditions-dependent complication, recorded because it changed a party's day: at least one party found the easy line broke into a fresh rockfall scar about 30 ft below the summit ridge and backed off rather than cross it, returning with a rope for about two pitches of juggy 5.7. Do not commit to the last 100 ft until you can see it.

The moat at the col is the thing to scout on the way up: where the snow meets the rock it is a non-event when snow-filled early season and can be an overhanging pit by August. Note where you crossed it; you will want that on the way down.

bivy.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
bivy.permit: This is the separate Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
bivy.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is legally awkward: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is not on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is walk-up only — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Stump Hollow bench
bivy.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
bivy.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

bivy.name: High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
bivy.notes: The western summits — the Twin Needles, Ottohorn, Himmelhorn and Frenzel Spitz — are far enough along the crest that a party working from a basin camp faces a very long day, so some take a bivouac high on the traverse instead. These are improvised spots rather than established sites, and quality varies from a decent gravel bench to a night sitting on a ledge. There is no shelter and no water, so this only makes sense with a settled forecast and a party willing to move fast the next morning.
bivy.water: No dependable source. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs: carry water up or melt snow, and expect nothing at all once the summer snow has gone.
bivy.permit: Still inside a cross-country zone and still requires a wilderness permit with the night assigned to the correct zone. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, keep 100 ft from water, no fires, and carry waste out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: One party, and often only a ledge or a gravel patch for two people

backups.approach: This is on the East Face, so — like Liberty Crack — the approach is not from the Blue Lake Trailhead but from a separate pullout on SR-20 at the hairpin curve just east of Washington Pass. Park on the north shoulder near the curve, walk back toward the pass to a small pond on the south side of the highway, round its east end, and follow a cairned boot path north into the forest. The path climbs through timber and breaks out onto the talus field directly below the East Face after roughly 20-30 minutes and 0.5 mile (~600-800 ft gain). No water source along the way; watch for the cairned track being hard to follow in low light, and loose talus underfoot at the base.
backups.descent_text: Because this is a shorter (4-pitch) line on the East Face rather than a full summit route like Liberty Crack or Thin Red Line, the standard descent is the same notch-based line used across Liberty Bell: downclimb east ~100 ft through trees/loose rock to the 2-bolt station, then one rappel to an intermediate stance followed by a double-rope rappel (or two single-rope raps) into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch — 2 rappels on bolted anchors — then downclimb the scree gully to the climbers' path. Note that because this route (like Liberty Crack) is approached from the East Face pullout rather than Blue Lake Trailhead, returning via the west-side notch means either a car shuttle or a roughly 1-mile roadside walk back to your vehicle; parties who top out near Liberty Crack's finish sometimes instead use that route's dedicated 6-bolt rap line or the 4-double-rope-rap line off M&M Ledge to return directly to the East Face base.

It climbs steeply through timber and comes out on the talus directly beneath the East Face in roughly half an hour to an hour.

approach_variants.baseFinding: The East Face carries a dense cluster of routes in a short stretch of wall, so identify your line off the big features before you leave the talus rather than by picking the nearest crack. The reference point everybody uses is the large roof high on the left-hand part of the wall — the Lithuanian Lip — which Liberty Crack passes on its right. Anything you start well right of that roof-and-crack system is a different route. Approach ledges at the base are third and fourth class and traverse in from the left, so the start of a line is usually a short sideways walk from where the talus meets the rock, not straight up from it.

There are no facilities and no water; it is a place to sleep in or beside the car, not a campsite. Highway 20 is closed through the winter, so this is unavailable until the road reopens.

backups.overview: Lexington Tower's East Face is a striking 10-pitch alpine rock climb on the prominent east wall of the Liberty Bell skyline, featuring an exposed no-hands traverse, a crux lieback, and memorable offwidth pitches including one with a jammed 2x4 for pro.
backups.beta: Start on low-angle dihedral left of Lexington-Minuteman gully. Ascend via cracks and chimneys; crux is pitch 5 with exposed traverse. Upper pitches are off-width and chimney climbing. Exit via notch, descend west gully. Standard trad rack essential; doubles to #3 plus a #4, with a single #5 or #6 useful for the short wide sections.
backups.turnaround: If the base snowfield or weather looks marginal, reconsider; the route is long for its grade.
backups.rappels: 0 — the standard descent is a walk-off down a short 3rd-class gully from the notch; no rappels required. A ~7-rappel line straight down the face is a documented but non-standard alternative some parties use in bad weather.
backups.permit: No climbing or wilderness permit required; Northwest Forest Pass (or day fee) to park at developed trailheads.
backups.comms: Cell service unreliable. Satellite communicator (Garmin InReach, PLB) recommended.
backups.descent: From the notch below the summit, descend west into the skier's-left gully and traverse north to the Liberty Bell cattle trail back to the Blue Lake trail.

sectionBreakdown.note: A long single day up straightforward, well-featured cracks, chimneys, and offwidths on Lexington's 800-ft east wall. Approach is short and quick; the climbing itself is the crux of…

backups.detailed_rack: A standard rack with gear to 6 inches; a #4 Camalot gets used a lot and a 6-inch piece helps the wide sections, though confident wide-crack climbers can skip it. Two newer bolts protect the offwidth pitch with the jammed 2x4. Bring long runners.
what_to_bring: helmet
60m rope
approach shoes
wide cams
headlamp
pro_tips: A wedged piece of 2x4 in the offwidth crack functions as fixed pro on one of the wide pitches — back it up, don't rely on it alone.
Bring a real #4 Camalot (or two); it sees repeated use through the wide pitches, while a single #6 covers the widest slot for parties who don't want to stem past it.
The crux comes at pitch 5 — an exposed traverse into a lieback — and the offwidth pitch above it has two bolts alongside the 2x4 for extra protection.
backups.pro_needs: Wide-friendly rack; the crux lieback and offwidth pitches reward big gear.
backups.best_season: Late June through September once the base snowfield recedes.
backups.approach: Park at the pond pullout on the south side of SR-20, about 1.2 miles east of Washington Pass (a small dirt turnout marked by a roadside pond). The climbers' path starts just left (west) of the highway's east-side guardrail/barrier and immediately begins gaining elevation through forest. It pops out of the trees onto an open scree-and-boulder slope that climbs directly toward the Liberty Bell group towers, with Lexington Tower's east face visible above. Figure 30-45 minutes (some parties report closer to an hour) of steep hiking/scrambling from the pullout to the base of the wall, gaining several hundred feet over roughly a third of a mile. There are two common ways to gain the actual start depending on snow coverage: a gully/snowfield left of the face, or scrambling in from climber's right on rock. Early-to-mid season the approach gully can hold firm snow well into summer (ice axe/traction useful); by late August it is typically dry talus and easily avoided. No reliable water source on this short approach — carry what you need from the car.
backups.descent_text: The standard descent is a walk-off, not a rappel-the-face descent. From the notch below the true summit (not the summit itself), head west and downclimb a short gully on skier's left — roughly 20 feet of 3rd-class terrain. Old rap slings are present in this gully but most parties simply downclimb rather than bother rigging a rappel. From the base of the gully, traverse right (north) until you intersect the well-worn climbers'/cattle trail that also serves Liberty Bell, and follow it down to join the Blue Lake Trail. Lower down, watch for a faint climbers' path that cuts back toward the highway and saves close to a mile of road-walking versus following Blue Lake Trail all the way to its own trailhead. Some parties instead choose to rappel directly back down the East Face route itself (useful in bad weather or if the walk-off is unfamiliar/snow-covered) — one documented descent of the face took 7 double-rope (60m) rappels, built from a mix of slung horns/rap rings and a couple of fixed/bolted anchors encountered on route. That face-rappel line is not the recommended standard descent, just an alternative to the normal walk-off descent.
backups.bail: Belay options are plentiful and pitches can be linked or reversed; the descent gully also provides an escape from the notch.

Up and slightly right to the base of an obvious left-facing corner; tree belay.
Climb the left-facing corner to a ledge with a tree belay.
Up and left through hand-to-finger cracks to a stance below a roof and a dead-end chimney.
Route crux: an exposed no-hands traverse right for 30 feet, then a difficult lieback into a hand/finger crack.
Offwidth climbing past a jammed 2x4 (fixed pro) and two bolts to an alcove.
Short chimney leads to blockier terrain and another offwidth section.
Easier low-fifth-class rock trending up and left past a few blocky steps; many parties simul-climb this section to save time before the upper headwall.
Continue on moderate terrain toward a tree belay.
Exposed catwalk traverse to the notch below the true summit, where the route unropes for the walk-off descent.

approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is a treed ledge, and there are two ways onto it and snow decides which. From the talus, either climb a roped 5.8 pitch around a protruding block, or scramble one of the gullies flanking the ledge. Snow lingering in the talus and at the base of the wall into early-mid summer affects whether you gain the ledge from the left or the right.

So the arrival test is a ledge with trees on it, part way up the wall, not ground level. Trees underfoot on a bench beneath a steep east-facing wall is the confirmation, and it works without seeing the tower above.

The discriminator against the other route from the same ledge, and it is a left-right test: Tooth and Claw begins near the left side of the treed ledge and angles rightward across slabs to its first bolt. If you are traversing right across slabs looking for a bolt, you are on Tooth and Claw, a 5.12a, not on the East Face.

Helmet up before the gullies, not after: both gullies flanking the ledge see fairly frequent rockfall.

Where the day ends, which is on the other side of the ridge: the standard descent is a walk-off from the notch below the true summit, not from the summit itself. Head west and downclimb a short gully on skier's left, about twenty feet of third class; old rap slings are present but most parties downclimb. From the base of that gully, traverse right, north, until you intersect the well-worn climbers' and cattle trail that also serves Liberty Bell, and follow it down to the Blue Lake Trail. Lower down, watch for a faint climbers' path that cuts back toward the highway and saves close to a mile of road walking.

bivy.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside bivy
bivy.notes: The usual answer for a car-to-car day on this group, and the start of every west-side approach, about a mile west of Washington Pass. Parties routinely sleep at the lot or at the highway hairpin rather than walking in, because the approaches are short enough that a high camp buys little. There are no facilities and no water; it is a place to sleep in or beside the car, not a campsite. Highway 20 is closed through the winter, so this is unavailable until the road reopens.
bivy.water: None at the trailhead. Carry what you need.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park
bivy.capacity: Informal, at the parking area — no prepared sites
